doc.title: Phil Mead interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

title: Father's piano, first saxophone lessons, and Donny James's band
summary: His father's jazz piano and soprano sax, Depression-era lessons on his father's saxophone, and being recruited at twelve for a Schenectady dance band.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: Right. Well my daughter actually did a little research for me and she came up with some of the top ten hits of around the mid-fifties. And they have such songs as “Oh My Papa” by Eddie Fisher and “Don’t Let the Stars Get in Your Eyes,” Perry Como, “That’s Amore,” Dean Martin. And then even into the rock & roll era with Bill Haley and the Comets. Now nowhere on this list are any Dixieland hits. So tell me why you came to Hamilton and were able to find people like yourself who were still into that music.
Well let me go back a little bit —

— in my history. My dad, who actually was a great runner, qualified for the 1928 Olympics, went to Wesleyan, but loved music. And was a pretty decent soprano saxophone player. You can relate to that, had a nice Buescher soprano saxophone which he played at Wesleyan. He graduated in 1928. But then he became a self-taught jazz piano player and was actually a very good piano player. And my earliest remembrances are dad, when he’d come home from work at night, he would play the piano. And he would play all the great old tunes. “Jada” and “Curse of an Aching Heart” and on and on, all the great old Dixie tunes. And as a child I just grew up with that. And I used to hum those tunes just because I heard them all the time. We then moved to — we moved around a lot. My dad worked for the telephone company in Upstate New York and was moved every few years. We then moved to Syracuse and when I was about ten they gave free music lessons at Edward Smith Junior High School in Syracuse. And I wanted to take trombone lessons. But you had to furnish your own instrument and we were careful with our money as Depression Era families were, and so he said, “Well you can take my saxophone.” So I learned to play the saxophone and actually became pretty good at it. So then he got me a tenor sax. And by then we had moved to Schenectady. And they have some good musicians in Schenectady including a band, Donny James and his Orchestra. High school kids, very good. This was around 1948 to 50. I was around ten or twelve. And of course those were the great swing bands, Glen Gray and all of that, and they had all those charts. And so the tenor player in this dance band was a catcher and he couldn’t play in the summer so I got recruited even though I was only twelve. And I could read like crazy. I couldn’t solo very well but I could read like crazy. So I was sitting up there
